claims.text: Local chemical heterogeneity is the dominant factor governing premelting onset and complete melting in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Equiatomic, chemically disordered HEA nanoparticles possess a broad distribution of local bonding environments because they contain multiple principal elements.
Controlled pre-annealing or selective element pairing can reduce local compositional fluctuations while retaining the same overall composition and particle-size distribution.
Chemical heterogeneity introduces spatial fluctuations in local atomic bond strengths.
Chemical heterogeneity introduces spatial fluctuations in interatomic diffusion barriers.
Regions with greater chemical heterogeneity have lower local melting thresholds because of variable bond energies.
Low-threshold heterogeneous regions undergo early surface disordering that propagates into complete melting.
Reducing chemical heterogeneity produces more uniform bond strengths.
Reducing chemical heterogeneity raises the onset temperature for premelting.
Nanoparticles with greater local chemical heterogeneity will premelt earlier than otherwise matched homogenized nanoparticles.
Nanoparticles with greater local chemical heterogeneity will have a lower complete melting temperature than otherwise matched homogenized nanoparticles.
The proposed relationship should hold for HEA nanoparticles between 5 and 50 nm.
The proposed relationship should hold during heating under inert or reducing environments.
The proposed relationship applies broadly to HEA nanoparticles intended for catalysis, sensing, energy storage, and corrosion-related applications.
Minor particle-size variations and interfacial-energy effects may confound measured premelting and melting-temperature shifts.
